H.G. Wells. Herbert George Wells, an English author whose scientific romances defined the trajectory of science fiction in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. His works explored the social and philosophical consequences of scientific advancement, imagining alien invasion, time travel, and biological manipulation with prescient concern for human nature and power. He bridged Victorian society and the modern anxious future. Wells wrote The Time Machine in 1895, imagining a future divided into the Eloi and Morlocks—a meditation on class stratification and evolutionary devolution. He created The War of the Worlds in 1898, depicting a Martian invasion of England and pioneering the alien-invasion narrative as a vehicle for social critique. His 1897 work The Invisible Man explored the moral corrosion of power and invisibility as metaphor for the powerless individual against society. In The Island of Doctor Moreau, published in 1896, he featured human-animal hybrids and interrogated the ethics of scientific experimentation and dominion over nature. Wells produced extensively across multiple genres—sociological essays, futuristic romances, and moral fables—grounding his speculation in contemporary concerns. His work was foundational to science fiction as a vehicle for social and philosophical exploration, not mere technological novelty.
